result.wellness_score_help_text:
The Wellness Score predicts cardiovascular risk for the next 5–10 years. It is calculated from measured vital signs and is intended as a reference when measured at rest under similar conditions with consistent results over time.

A higher Wellness Score indicates lower cardiovascular risk.

How is it calculated?
Your Wellness Score is calculated using your vitals results from any single measurement. The values of each vital sign measurement affect your Wellness Score prediction.

Generally, a lower resting Heart Rate implies more efficient heart function and better cardiovascular fitness. Therefore, a higher Heart Rate reduces your Wellness Score—even when the heart rate is within the normal range. For example, heart rates higher than 65 reduce the wellness score to a medium score, and values higher than 84 reduce the score to a low score.

HRV measures the variation in time between heartbeats. The Stress Level calculated from this variance also affects your Wellness Score. Thus, Very High and High stress levels are correlated with a low score, while Mild and Normal stress levels are correlated with a medium score.

Your Oxygen Saturation level measures the amount of oxygen in the blood delivered from the lungs to the rest of the body. A higher level implies more efficient function, thus a lower Oxygen Saturation level reduces the Wellness Score.

In addition, high Blood Pressure readings at rest may pose a higher risk of health problems and therefore may reduce the Wellness Score.

Measured indicators are not for medical use.

info.heart_rate_body: Heart Rate is the number of times your heart beats per minute. The normal resting rate is 60 to 100 bpm. A higher resting heart rate may indicate stress or other conditions and can increase cardiovascular risk over time.
info.breathing_rate_body: Breathing Rate is the number of breaths you take per minute. The normal at-rest breathing rate is 12 to 20 breaths per minute. It can change with activity, emotions, medications, and medical conditions.
info.prq_body: PRQ (Pulse-Respiration Quotient) is the ratio between heart rate and breathing rate. A normal PRQ is around 5. A large deviation may indicate inefficient cardio-respiratory balance.
info.oxygen_saturation_body: Oxygen Saturation measures how much oxygen the blood carries from the lungs to the body. Normal levels are typically 95–100%. Lower values may indicate respiratory or circulatory issues.
info.blood_pressure_body: Blood Pressure is the pressure of blood against artery walls, expressed as systolic/diastolic. Normal systolic pressure is 100–129. Consistently high values can increase cardiovascular risk.
info.stress_level_body: Stress Level is derived from Heart Rate Variability (HRV). Higher stress levels reflect higher sympathetic nervous system activity.
info.hrv_sdnn_body: SDNN is the standard deviation of normal-to-normal RR intervals and is a common HRV metric. Higher SDNN often reflects better recovery and resilience.
info.mean_rri_body: Mean RRi is the average time between RR intervals. A longer Mean RRi indicates a lower heart rate and higher parasympathetic activity.
info.rmssd_body: RMSSD is a time-domain HRV metric representing beat-to-beat variability. Higher values are associated with relaxation.
info.sd1_body: SD1 represents short-term variability in the Poincaré plot.
info.sd2_body: SD2 represents long-term variability in the Poincaré plot.
info.pns_zone_body:
PNS stands for the Parasympathetic Nervous System. The PNS Zone indicates which range (Zone) your parasympathetic activity falls into.

High: Your body is relaxed and recovering well.

Low: Your body is not getting enough rest or your recovery is reduced.
info.pns_index_body:
PNS stands for the Parasympathetic Nervous System. The PNS Index is a numerical score showing how actively your parasympathetic system is working.

Think of it as a brake performance score. Just as a car needs strong brakes to stop and refuel, your body needs a higher PNS to recharge.

High: The brakes are working very well. Your body is deeply relaxed, recovering quickly, digestion is good, and sleep is likely better.

Low: The brakes are weak or not engaging. Even when resting, your body stays tense and recovery is limited. High stress can lower this score.

Summary: During exercise/work, SNS (accelerator) should be high and PNS (brake) low. During rest/sleep, SNS should be low and PNS high. If your PNS stays low while resting, consider deep breathing or meditation to relax.
info.sns_index_body: SNS stands for the Sympathetic Nervous System. The SNS Index is a numerical score indicating how strongly your sympathetic system is activated. Higher values suggest your body is tense, excited, or under stress.
info.sns_zone_body:
SNS Zone is a staged interpretation of the SNS Index.

Low: Very calm and relaxed.

Normal: Appropriate tension for daily activity.

High: Under stress or physically demanding state.

Extreme: Excessive stress or physical overload.

wellness_info.wellness_index_definition_text: A composite predictive risk score calculated by combining various health indicators such as cardiovascular risk.
wellness_info.wellness_index_purpose_text: The purpose is to predict the risk of cardiovascular diseases that may occur within 5 to 10 years and encourage users to take preventive measures.
wellness_info.wellness_index_display_text: Usually displayed as a numerical value (Score) such as '7/10'.
wellness_info.wellness_level_definition_text: The measured index or risk level is classified into three stages: Low, Medium, and High, so that users can understand it at a glance.
wellness_info.wellness_level_role_text: Converts the user's current status based on numerical data (e.g., 4/10) into intuitive feedback.
wellness_info.wellness_level_usage_text: This level information is directly displayed to end users or delivered to insurance underwriting teams, and is used as a basis for decision-making, such as recommending additional medical examinations when the risk level is high.
